text: Grid search is thorough, but the cost multiplies with every hyperparameter you add. This lesson covers two ways to search smarter: random search, which you can use today, and Bayesian search, which learns as it goes.

Grid search tries every combination on your list. Random search draws a fixed number of combinations from distributions you describe. Bayesian search goes further: it uses the scores of earlier trials to decide what to try next.

For random search you describe ranges instead of lists. Scipy's randint draws whole numbers, so trees between fifty and four hundred, depth between three and twenty-nine, and leaf size between one and nine. A plain list, like max_features, is sampled evenly.

RandomizedSearchCV takes the model, the distributions, and n_iter, the number of combinations to try. We ask for twenty, with five-fold cross-validation, so that is one hundred fits. The best is depth seventeen, max_features point eight, leaf size one, and ninety-nine trees, with a cross-validated F1 of point nine two.

Look at the top of cv_results_. The top five all land between point nine one one and point nine two, with different settings each. Random search found a good region without trying everything. A grid over these same ranges would have three hundred forty thousand two hundred combinations. The refit winner scores point nine two seven F1 on the test set.

For continuous hyperparameters like C or a learning rate, sample on a log scale with scipy's loguniform. Values between point zero zero one and one hundred get equal odds per power of ten, instead of nearly all draws landing above ten.

Bayesian optimization is the idea behind libraries such as Optuna and scikit-optimize. Score a few settings, fit a cheap model of score versus settings, pick the next trial where a good score looks likely, and repeat until your budget runs out. It pays off when each fit is expensive. We are not running one here, so check each library's current docs and supported versions.
Next, lesson fifteen: why the best cross-validated score is too optimistic, and how to avoid overfitting the validation set.
